description: through our project, “Abandoned but Not Forgotten,” we explore NASA’s equipment on the Moon, Mars, and beyond. We aim to discover the missions, scientific contributions, and stories behind these forgotten explorers. By sharing what we learn, we hope to inspire other students to look beyond Earth and dream of becoming the explorers of tomorrow.
summary:
Project Summary, Purpose, and Significance
The Sounds of Tranquility Base is a browser-based, interactive 3D educational project designed to introduce children to the NASA hardware left on the lunar surface during the Apollo 11 mission. The primary purpose of the project is to spark children's interest in space exploration and help them learn scientific concepts through an engaging story.

The target audience of the project consists primarily of school-aged space enthusiasts. By exploring a 3D lunar model, children can discover the equipment, listen to their stories, and participate in interactive activities such as laser ranging and moonquakes.

The significance of the project lies in combining astronomy, engineering, and science to provide children with a lasting and enjoyable learning experience. Furthermore, it supports scientific accuracy by utilizing real NASA data, teaching children how to research, question, and wonder. With its accessible and bilingual structure, it ensures that diverse learners can benefit from this experience.

In short: This project aims not only to inform children about space, but also to encourage them to think like the scientists of the future.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
“Sounds of Tranquility Base” is a single-file, interactive 3D experience that lets students explore the journey of Apollo 11 right in their web browser. Nothing needs to be installed. Users start with a rotating Moon and read Apollo 11’s story in six chapters: liftoff, the trip to the Moon, the landing, the first step, 2.5 hours at Tranquility Base, and the return home. Then they “land” at Tranquility Base and play four missions on the lunar surface:

  • Eagle: pack the cargo for liftoff and fire the engine at the right moment.
  • Laser reflector: guess how long light takes to travel to the Moon and back, then measure it.
  • Seismometer: a “detective” game that identifies the source of a moonquake from the shape of its signal.
  • Plaque: decode the parts of the plaque, answer questions, and write your own plaque.

Users can also visit 20 other lunar landing and abandoned-spacecraft sites (Apollo 12–17, Surveyor, Lunokhod, Odysseus, and more). The lunar ground is built from a real 3D terrain model, with craters, rocks, footprints and realistic shadows. The app works in Turkish and English.

Benefits

  • It turns space history, which can feel dry, into a game. Each game teaches a scientific concept: mass and fuel, the speed of light and distance measurement, seismic waves, and communication.
  • After each mission, students earn badges and stars. Collecting all four badges completes the mission.
  • Fact boxes and NASA source links let students reach accurate information while having fun.

Intended impact
To spark curiosity about space science in children and students, and to help them enjoy learning by discovery. It can be used as classroom material, at home, or at a science fair. Because it is a single file, it is easy to share.

Tools and technologies used

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no additional framework.
  • Three.js for 3D graphics and Tailwind CSS for the interface.
  • HTML5 Canvas and SVG for the seismogram and visuals.
  • A 3D lunar-ground model in 3DS format for the terrain, converted into a height map with Python (NumPy, SciPy) and embedded in the code.
  • Data and photographs taken from NASA records.
  • An AI assistant (Claude) and automated browser tests (Playwright) were used during coding and testing. The Earth–Moon image in the journey chapter is an illustration generated with Gemini, and this is clearly stated in the project.

Creativity

  • Story, 3D world and games come together in a single user flow. Students read the story, “land” on the Moon, and apply what they learned on site.
  • The games are based on real facts. For example, at liftoff the dust flies in straight arcs because there is no air, and the exhaust knocks the flag over. The seismometer shakes in the scene.
  • Game formats such as the “detective” who reads seismograms and writing your own plaque make learning personal.

Factors considered

  • Age-appropriateness: short sentences, emojis, large buttons, and retrying without penalty.
  • Accuracy: information is linked to NASA sources. Simplified values, such as the cargo weights in the game, are marked as “rounded for the game”.
  • Accessibility: a reduce-motion setting, keyboard and screen-reader support, and mobile-friendly layout.
  • Ease of access: multilingual, no installation, a single file.
